mainEntity.name: Why do Meta and Google both report the same sale?

acceptedAnswer.text: Each counts conversions it can link to its own ads, using its own rules. A customer who touched both can be counted by both.
Start from real orders in your store. Use blended ROAS as the headline and platform numbers as direction.
Total revenue divided by total ad spend across every channel. Because it does not depend on who claims credit, it cannot double count.

mainEntity.name: Does the Conversions API fix over-counting?

acceptedAnswer.text: It does not remove overlap, but it gives platforms more complete data, which improves reporting and optimisation.

acceptedAnswer.text: Pause it for a planned period or run a holdout, and watch total orders. The change shows what it added.

hub.sub: Each platform reports the conversions it can link to its own ads. Add them up and they often exceed your real orders. Here is how to read the results anyway.

answer.label: In short
answer.lead: Attribution overlap is what happens when several platforms each claim credit for the same sale, so the reported total is larger than the orders you actually received.
answer.hl: several platforms each claim credit for the same sale
answer.who: Monday Marketing Company (MMC) starts from your store's orders, reads platform numbers as direction and not as totals, and sends cleaner signals back to the platforms with tools such as the Meta Conversions API.

cta.lede: On a call, with a senior strategist. We start from your store orders and read the platforms against them.

paras: A customer often sees an Instagram ad, later searches on Google, and buys after clicking an email. Each platform can legitimately claim that sale under its own rules, so each one reports it. Put the three reports side by side and you count the same sale three times.
Nothing is broken when this happens. The platforms are each answering a different question: which of my ads did this person interact with?
blocks.cap: Two ad platforms can both report the same purchase.

paras: The numbers below are made up to show the pattern. Your own will differ.

callout.title: What it shows
callout.text: The three reports add up to more than twice the real orders. Trusting any single dashboard, or adding them together, gives the wrong picture.

list: Each platform uses its own attribution settings and its own way of counting a conversion.
A person can touch several channels before buying, and more than one can claim the credit.
Privacy settings, blocked cookies and app-to-web journeys mean each platform sees only part of the journey.
Some reports count views as well as clicks, which widens what is credited to ads.

blocks.h: How to read your results anyway

steps.d: Your store admin holds the real orders and revenue. Treat it as the base every other number is compared with.
Divide total revenue by total ad spend across all channels. It ignores who claims credit, so it cannot double count.
Add a short 'How did you hear about us?' question after purchase. It catches channels that dashboards miss.
Within one platform, compare ads and audiences against each other. The comparison is useful even when the total is not exact.
Pause a channel for a planned period, or run a holdout, and watch total orders. The change shows what the channel really added.

blocks.cap: A post-purchase question adds a signal that dashboards cannot.

paras: Overlap is a measuring problem, and part of the fix is better data. Server-side tracking, such as the Meta Conversions API, sends purchase events from your server instead of relying only on the browser. That gives the platform a more complete view, which improves both reporting and the audiences it learns to find.
Clean event set-up in your analytics tool also helps you see the paths customers take before they buy.
blocks.cap: Analytics reports show the paths that lead to a purchase.

paras: Track blended ROAS as the headline, use platform numbers to compare ads within a platform, and use surveys and switch-off tests to check the big spending decisions. Read all of it against your break-even ROAS, so the answer is whether the campaign makes money, not whether a dashboard looks good.
blocks.cap: Blended ROAS is total revenue divided by total ad spend.
